\chapter{Beautiful, and Not}
\label{ch:ml-beauty}
\hlchaptermodality{97}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can say that something is beautiful, name beauty itself, and deny it.}

From cold: both ends of one quality, and which letter arrives when aaNu follows a word.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[sundaraṁ]{\ml{സുന്ദരം} (sundaraṁ) — beautiful}

\label{lesson:ML-C97-sundaram}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{this is easy}. You built that sentence one chapter ago.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\textbf{\ml{സുന്ദരം}} — \emph{sundaraṁ} — \textbf{beautiful.}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ml{ഇത്} \ml{സുന്ദരമാണ്}.} — \emph{itŭ sundaramāṇŭ} — \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{This is beautiful.}\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
\textbf{Read what you just did.} The word ends in \textbf{\ml{ം}}, so it welds onto \textbf{\ml{ആണ്}} the way the last chapter's two words did, and you did it without being told.

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{} & \textbf{} \\
\midrule
\textbf{\ml{ഇത്} \ml{എളുപ്പമാണ്}} & this is easy \\
\textbf{\ml{ഇത്} \ml{സുന്ദരമാണ്}} & this is beautiful \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

That is what a frame is for. \textbf{The chapter before this one cost you a rule; this one costs you a word}, and the rule is still doing the work.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{sundaraṁ}
  \item \emph{itŭ sundaramāṇŭ}
  \item the same sentence about something being easy
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What is \emph{beautiful}? (\textbf{\ml{സുന്ദരം}}.) Did you need a new rule to say \emph{this is beautiful}? (\textbf{No} — it ends in \textbf{\ml{ം}}, like the last two.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[bhaṅgi]{\ml{ഭംഗി} (bhaṅgi) — beauty}

\label{lesson:ML-C97-bhangi}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{this is beautiful}. Then say \emph{child} — you have had that word a long time.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\textbf{\ml{ഭംഗി}} — \emph{bhaṅgi} — \textbf{beauty}, the thing itself rather than the quality.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ml{ഇത്} \ml{ഭംഗിയാണ്}.} — \emph{itŭ bhaṅgiyāṇŭ} — \textquotedblleft{}This is beauty.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{This one does not end in \ml{ം}, and it shows.} Read the two welds side by side:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{} & \textbf{} \\
\midrule
\textbf{\ml{സുന്ദരം}} $\to$ \textbf{\ml{സുന്ദരമാണ്}} & a \textbf{\ml{മ}} appears \\
\textbf{\ml{ഭംഗി}} $\to$ \textbf{\ml{ഭംഗിയാണ്}} & a \textbf{\ml{യ}} appears \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

You have seen the second one before, on a word you learned long ago: \textbf{\ml{ഇത്} \ml{എന്റെ} \ml{കുട്ടിയാണ്}} — \emph{this is my child.}

\textbf{Neither word loses anything.} A letter arrives to carry the vowel of \textbf{\ml{ആണ്}}, and which letter arrives depends on how the word ended. That is the whole difference.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{bhaṅgi}, then \emph{bhaṅgiyāṇŭ}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{sundaraṁ}, then \emph{sundaramāṇŭ}
  \item \emph{Look:} at the two joined forms, and name the letter that differs
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What is \emph{beauty}? (\textbf{\ml{ഭംഗി}}.) Which letter appears when \textbf{\ml{ആണ്}} follows it? (\textbf{\ml{യ}}.) And after a word ending in \textbf{\ml{ം}}? (\textbf{\ml{മ}}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[itŭ sundaraṁ alla]{\ml{ഇത്} \ml{സുന്ദരം} \ml{അല്ല} (itŭ sundaraṁ alla) — this is not beautiful}

\label{lesson:ML-C97-alla-sundaram}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{this is beautiful}. Then say the word that denies being what you were called.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the denial stands apart}]
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ml{ഇത്} \ml{സുന്ദരം} \ml{അല്ല}.} — \emph{itŭ sundaraṁ alla} — \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{This is not beautiful.}\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

Look at what did \textbf{not} happen. \textbf{\ml{അല്ല}} did not weld onto the word in front of it, the way \textbf{\ml{ആണ്}} did. It stands on its own, after the thing being denied — exactly as you first met it:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{} & \textbf{} \\
\midrule
\textbf{\ml{ഞാൻ} \ml{അധ്യാപകൻ} \ml{അല്ല}} & I am not a teacher \\
\textbf{\ml{ഇത്} \ml{സുന്ദരം} \ml{അല്ല}} & this is not beautiful \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\textbf{Same shape, different subject.} The word being denied sits in the middle, unchanged and unwelded, and \textbf{\ml{സുന്ദരം}} keeps its \textbf{\ml{ം}} because nothing attached to it.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Both ends of the same line, from one new word and one you already had.

This is how the far end of most qualities will arrive for a while: \textbf{not by a second word, but by denying the first one.} It is what a learner can actually use early, and it is what a Malayalam speaker often says anyway.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{itŭ sundaramāṇŭ}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{itŭ sundaraṁ alla}
  \item \emph{Say it:} the two one after the other, and hear where they part
  \item \emph{Look:} at \textbf{\ml{സുന്ദരം}} in the second sentence, and say what happened to its \textbf{\ml{ം}}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
How do you say \emph{this is not beautiful}? (\textbf{\ml{ഇത്} \ml{സുന്ദരം} \ml{അല്ല}}.) Does \textbf{\ml{അല്ല}} weld onto the word before it? (\textbf{No} — it stands apart.) So what happens to the \textbf{\ml{ം}}? (\textbf{Nothing}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[sundaravuṁ allāthatuṁ enna ōrmma]{(beautiful, and not) — from cold}

\label{lesson:ML-R97-beauty-recall}



\begin{quote}
Close the lessons before this one. Say \emph{this is beautiful}, then deny it.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: which letter arrives}]
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{word} & \textbf{joined to \textbf{\ml{ആണ്}}} & \textbf{} \\
\midrule
\textbf{\ml{എളുപ്പം}} & \textbf{\ml{എളുപ്പമാണ്}} & \textbf{\ml{മ}} arrives \\
\textbf{\ml{സുന്ദരം}} & \textbf{\ml{സുന്ദരമാണ്}} & \textbf{\ml{മ}} arrives \\
\textbf{\ml{കുട്ടി}} & \textbf{\ml{കുട്ടിയാണ്}} & \textbf{\ml{യ}} arrives \\
\textbf{\ml{ഭംഗി}} & \textbf{\ml{ഭംഗിയാണ്}} & \textbf{\ml{യ}} arrives \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\textbf{Nothing is lost in any of the four.} A letter arrives to carry the vowel of \textbf{\ml{ആണ്}}, and \textbf{which one depends on how the word ended} — nothing else.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ml{ഇത്} \ml{സുന്ദരമാണ്}.} — this is beautiful.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ml{ഇത്} \ml{സുന്ദരം} \ml{അല്ല}.} — this is not beautiful.
\end{quote}

The second is not a second word. \textbf{\ml{അല്ല}} stands apart, the way it has since you first met it, and \textbf{\ml{സുന്ദരം}} keeps its \textbf{\ml{ം}} because nothing attached.

So one new quality gave you both ends of a line. That is how the far end of most qualities will arrive for a while — \textbf{by denying the near one}, which is both what you can build today and what a speaker often says anyway.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{sundaraṁ} $\to$ \emph{sundaramāṇŭ}
  \item \emph{bhaṅgi} $\to$ \emph{bhaṅgiyāṇŭ}
  \item \emph{itŭ sundaraṁ alla}
  \item which of the two joined forms takes a \textbf{\ml{യ}}, and why
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Beautiful, and beauty? (\textbf{\ml{സുന്ദരം}, \ml{ഭംഗി}}.) Which letter arrives on each before \textbf{\ml{ആണ്}}? (\textbf{\ml{മ}} and \textbf{\ml{യ}}.) And how do you deny it? (\textbf{\ml{ഇത്} \ml{സുന്ദരം} \ml{അല്ല}} — \ml{അല്ല} standing apart.)
\end{tcolorbox}
